A lawyer agreed the great law was to love God and love your neighbor. Then, to test Jesus, he asked, “And who is my neighbor?”
Jesus didn’t give a definition. He told a story. A man was going down the road from Jerusalem to Jericho, and robbers left him half dead.
A priest came by, saw him, and passed by on the other side. Then a Levite, a temple helper, did the same.
Then a Samaritan, from a people many listeners mistrusted, saw him and was moved with compassion. He bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine.
He took him to an inn and paid for his care. “Look after him. Whatever more you spend, I’ll repay you when I return.”
“Which of these three was a neighbor to the man?” “The one who showed mercy.” Jesus said, “Go and do the same.”
Jesus told a story. A young man said to his father, “Give me my share of what’s coming to me.”
So the father divided what he had.
Not many days later, the younger son packed everything and left for a far country.
There he wasted it all on wild living.
Then a severe famine came over that country, and he began to be in need.
He took a job feeding pigs. He longed to eat what the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.
Then he came to himself.
He set off for home, practicing his speech: “Father, I have sinned. Make me one of your hired servants.”
But while he was still far off, his father saw him.
He was moved with compassion. He ran, threw his arms around him, and kissed him.
The son began his speech. The father didn’t let him finish.
“Bring out the best robe. Put a ring on his hand. Let’s celebrate. He was lost, and is found.”

Corinth was a busy Greek port city. A small church there followed Jesus, rich and poor, sharing one table.
Then the trouble started. They split into camps, “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos.” Some even took each other to court.
Paul heard the news far away in Ephesus. He sent them a long letter. And right in the middle of it, he wrote about love.
“Love is patient. Love is kind. It doesn’t envy, it doesn’t boast, it isn’t proud. It keeps no record of wrongs.”
“It bears all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails.” Paul’s word for love was agape, the same word the Bible uses for God’s love.
A father brought his son to Jesus’s friends. Since childhood, the boy had suffered terrible fits. The friends tried to help, and couldn’t.
Jesus came down from a mountain into the middle of an argument. The father stepped forward: “If you can do anything, take pity on us and help us.”
“If you can?” said Jesus. “All things are possible for the one who believes.”
At once the father cried out, “I believe. Help my unbelief!”
Jesus spoke, and the boy grew still. Then Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he stood.
Even his closest friends wrestled with doubt. After Easter, on a mountain, the gospel says, “they worshiped him, but some doubted.”
Young David played music for King Saul. But as David became loved by the people, Saul grew jealous, and turned against him.
David ran for his life. For years he lived in the wilderness, hiding in caves, with the king’s soldiers on his trail.
The Bible keeps a book of songs, many linked to David, called psalms. Some were sung in the darkest times.
“How long, Lord? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?”
But the same short psalm ends, “I will sing to the Lord, because he has been good to me.”
In the Roman world, a cross wasn’t jewelry. It was a shameful death, kept for slaves, rebels and criminals.
Jesus was sentenced to die on one. A man coming in from the country, Simon of Cyrene, was made to carry the cross behind him.
On the cross, Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Below, the soldiers threw dice for his clothes.
One of the criminals beside him said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Jesus said, “Today you will be with me in paradise.”
At noon, darkness came over the land. Jesus cried out, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Then he died.
Most of his disciples had fled. But the women stayed, watching from a distance, and saw where he was laid.
Early on Sunday, at sunrise, three women walked to Jesus’s tomb with spices. His other friends were hiding. The women came.
On the way they worried: “Who will roll away the stone for us?” It was very big.
But when they looked up, the stone had already been rolled back.
Inside sat a young man in white. “Don’t be afraid. You’re looking for Jesus, who was crucified. He has risen. He is not here.”
Mary Magdalene stayed by the tomb, crying. She saw a man nearby and thought he was the gardener.
Then he said one word: “Mary.” She turned, and knew him. She ran to tell the others, “I have seen the Lord!”
Priscilla and Aquila were a Jewish couple, tentmakers. When the emperor forced Jews out of Rome, they packed up and moved to Corinth.
Then Paul arrived, a tentmaker too. He lived with them, and the three of them sewed tents side by side.
In Ephesus they heard a gifted preacher, Apollos. Instead of correcting him in public, they took him aside and explained the way of God more fully.
People gathered in their home to pray and share bread. Paul wrote, “Greet the church that is in their house.”
Paul said they were like one body: eyes, hands, feet, every part needed. “You are the body of Christ.”

21.title: the beginning of the good news

shots.cap: The shortest of the four gospels doesn’t start with a manger. It starts, “The beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ.”
In the desert by the Jordan River, a wild prophet named John, dressed in camel’s hair, called people to turn back to God.
Crowds came from Jerusalem and all the countryside, and he baptized them in the river.
“Someone is coming after me who is greater than I am,” John said. Then one day Jesus came from Nazareth, and was baptized too.
As he came up out of the water, the sky tore open and the Spirit came down on him like a dove. And a voice spoke.
From there the story runs. “Immediately” comes again and again, on a road that leads all the way to Jerusalem.

So many people came that Jesus got into a boat and sat on the water, while the crowd stood on the shore. He told them a story.
“A farmer went out to sow.” He threw his seed by hand, far and wide.
Some fell on the path, and birds ate it. Some fell on rocky ground. It sprang up fast, then withered in the sun.
Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it.
But some fell on good soil, and brought a harvest: a hundred, sixty, or thirty times what was sown.
Jesus said the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, one of the smallest seeds a farmer would plant.
But when it grows, it’s bigger than all the garden plants. It becomes a tree, and the birds come and nest in its branches.
Then another story. The kingdom is like yeast that a woman hid in three measures of flour.
Three measures was a huge amount, enough bread for a crowd. A pinch of yeast, hidden inside, lifted all of it.
Small, and hidden. That’s how Jesus said God’s kingdom starts.
Tax collectors and outsiders crowded around Jesus. Some religious leaders grumbled, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.”
So Jesus told them a story. “Which of you, with a hundred sheep, if you lose one, doesn’t leave the ninety-nine and go after the lost one?”
He goes out into the wild hills, and he keeps searching until he finds it.
And when he finds it, he doesn’t scold it. He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and carries it home.
He calls his friends and neighbors: “Rejoice with me!” Jesus said heaven rejoices like that over one lost person who turns back to God.
Right after the lost sheep, Jesus told another story. A woman had ten silver coins, each about a day’s pay. Then she lost one.
She didn’t wait for morning. She lit a lamp.
She swept the whole house, corner by corner, and searched carefully until she found it.
There it was, in the dust. She held it up in the lamplight.
Then she called her friends and neighbors: “Rejoice with me! I’ve found the coin I lost.”
Jesus said the kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field. In those days, people buried valuables to keep them safe.
A man found it. It wasn’t his field. He covered it up again.
“Then in his joy he goes and sells everything he has, and buys that field.”
Again: a merchant looking for fine pearls found one of great price. He sold everything he had and bought it.
Elsewhere Jesus said, “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
A landowner went out at dawn to hire workers for his vineyard. He agreed to pay them a denarius, the usual day’s wage.
He went back at nine, at noon, and at three, and hired more.
At five, an hour before quitting time, he found others still standing around. “No one has hired us.” “You go into the vineyard too.”
The ones who came at five got a full day’s pay. The ones hired at dawn were sure they’d get more.
They got the same, and grumbled: “These last worked one hour, and you made them equal to us, who bore the heat of the day!”
“Friend, I’m doing you no wrong. Didn’t you agree to a denarius? Or are you envious because I am good?”

A huge crowd followed Jesus to a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee. Thousands of people, far from town, and nothing to eat.
His friend Andrew found one boy with five barley loaves and two fish. “But what are these among so many?”
He had everyone sit down on the grass. Then he took the boy’s loaves, gave thanks, and began handing them out.
Bread passed from hand to hand across the hillside. Everyone ate as much as they wanted.
Afterward he said, “Gather up the leftover pieces, so that nothing is lost.” They filled twelve baskets.
Today, in many Catholic homes, someone still stops the hands reaching for the bread. Heads bow. A few words before anyone eats.
In Nazareth, a small town in Galilee, lived a young woman named Mary. She was promised in marriage to a man named Joseph.
One ordinary day, the angel Gabriel came to her and said, “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.”
She was troubled. Gabriel said, “Do not be afraid, Mary, you have found grace with God. You will have a son, and name him Jesus.”
Mary asked an honest question: “How can this be?” She wasn’t married yet. Gabriel answered, “Nothing is impossible for God.”
Then Mary said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord. Be it done to me according to thy word.” And the angel left her.
Today, in many towns, church bells ring at morning, noon and evening. Some Catholics stop and pray the Angelus, remembering this very moment.

One day Jesus was praying by himself. When he finished, one of his friends said, “Lord, teach us to pray.”
He gave them a prayer that starts with a family word: “Father.” The version prayed at every Mass begins, “Our Father, who art in heaven.”
Then he told a story. A man knocks on his friend’s door at midnight: “Lend me three loaves. A guest has come, and I have nothing to give him.”
Because he kept knocking, the friend got up and gave him the bread. Then Jesus told his friends: ask, seek, knock.
“What father, if his child asks for a fish, hands him a snake? How much more will the Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask!”
Today, at every Mass, the whole room prays it together before communion. Not my Father. Our Father.

12.title: why everyone stands for a book

shots.cap: After years in exile, the people came home to Jerusalem. They gathered in a city square and asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the book of God’s law.
Ezra climbed a wooden platform, high above the crowd, so everyone could see: men, women, anyone old enough to understand.
When he opened the book, all the people stood up. He read aloud from early morning until noon, and helpers explained it so everyone understood.
As they heard the words, the whole crowd began to weep.
The leaders said, “This day is holy. Do not weep. Go, eat and drink, and send food to anyone who has none.” And the city celebrated.
Today, at Mass, people sit for the first readings. Then the whole room stands, often as the Gospel book is carried in, and the story of Jesus is read.
On the night of the first Easter, the friends of Jesus hid in a locked room. They had run away when he was arrested. Now they were afraid.
Then Jesus was standing among them, though the doors were locked. His first words were, “Peace be with you.”
He showed them his hands, and they were overjoyed. Then he said it again, “Peace be with you,” and gave the frightened friends a job.
Then he breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” The locked room was not the end of the story.
He had once taught: if you bring a gift to the altar and remember someone has something against you, leave it there. First make peace, then come back.
Today, just before communion at Mass, everyone turns to whoever is beside them, even a stranger, and says, “Peace be with you.”

14.title: one day that isn’t yours
14.told: a story of the martyrs of Abitinae

shots.cap: Around the year 304, in a North African town called Abitinae, the Roman emperor banned Christians from meeting. Their holy books were being taken away.
But every Sunday, a group of them still gathered in a house, with their priest, to share the Lord’s supper: the Mass.
Soldiers found them and took them to the city of Carthage, to stand before the Roman governor.
The governor asked why they had broken the emperor’s order. A man named Emeritus, who had opened his house to them, answered.
“Without Sunday, we cannot live.” Many of them never came home. But their words are still quoted by the Church today.
Today, the Church asks Catholics to keep Sunday: Mass on Sunday or Saturday evening, then rest, family, a long meal. Sickness or caring for someone excuses you.

15.title: why there’s fire in every church

shots.cap: Ireland, long ago. On a spring night, the High King at Tara ordered every fire in the land put out. No flame could burn before his own.
On the hill of Slane, Patrick, a missionary bishop, lit the Easter fire anyway. Across the dark valley, the king saw it blazing.
The king’s wise men warned him: if that fire is not put out tonight, it will never be put out.
Today, the Easter Vigil begins the same way: a new fire outside a dark church, and one tall candle lit from it, the Easter candle.
Candle to candle, the flame spreads through the crowd, until the whole dark church is full of light.
And in a side corner, rows of small candles. Someone lit one for a sick mother, a job interview, a friend who died. It keeps burning after they leave.
Very early on Sunday morning, after Jesus was buried, a few women walked to his tomb with spices, to care for his body. The apostles were not with them.
On the way, they worried. A huge stone sealed the tomb. “Who will roll the stone away for us?” They went anyway.
When they arrived, the stone was already rolled back. The tomb was empty.
Two men in dazzling clothes stood beside them. “Why do you look for the living among the dead? He is not here. He has risen.”
The women ran to tell the apostles. The men didn’t believe them at first. It sounded like nonsense.
Today, Easter isn’t one day. Catholics keep it for fifty days, longer than Lent. And every Sunday keeps a little of that morning.

17.title: the rich kid who gave his clothes back

shots.cap: Italy, about eight hundred years ago. In Assisi, a town on a hill, a rich cloth merchant’s son named Francis threw the best parties in town.
He dreamed of being a knight, rode off to war with the next town, and was captured. He came home from prison sick, and changed.
He began giving things away, even cloth from his father’s shop. His furious father dragged him before the bishop, in front of the whole town.
Francis took off his clothes and handed them to his father. “Until now I called you my father. From now on I’ll say: our Father in heaven.”
The bishop wrapped him in his own cloak. In those same years, Francis met a man with leprosy, someone everyone avoided. He got down and kissed his hand.
Friends joined him, living poor, preaching in the streets, caring for the sick. They became the Franciscans. Near the end, he wrote a song to God for “Brother Sun.”

18.title: the word pope francis kept saying

shots.cap: In the lakeside town of Capernaum sat a tax collector named Matthew, taking money for Rome. People saw men like him as traitors and cheats.
One day Jesus walked past his table, looked straight at him, and said two words: “Follow me.”
Matthew got up from his table, left it all behind, and followed him.
Soon Matthew’s house was full: tax collectors and sinners at dinner with Jesus. Some religious men grumbled, “Why does he eat with people like them?”
Centuries later, an English monk named Bede wrote about that moment: Jesus looked at Matthew with mercy, and chose him.
In 1953, a sixteen-year-old in Buenos Aires walked into a church on Saint Matthew’s day, went to confession, and felt that same look. He became Pope Francis.

19.title: one, holy, catholic
19.told: a story of Saint Ignatius of Antioch

shots.cap: Early in the 100s, Ignatius, the bishop of Antioch in Syria, was arrested for being a Christian and sent under guard to Rome.
Ten soldiers marched him across what is now Turkey. He called them his ten leopards: the more kindness they were shown, he wrote, the worse they got.
In the city of Smyrna, church after church sent people to meet him. Still in chains, Ignatius wrote them letters to carry home.
In one letter, he called the Church “catholic.” It’s the oldest writing we have that uses that word for the Church.
Then they sailed on toward Rome, where he died for his faith. His letters were copied and passed from church to church.
Today, Mass is said in Lagos, Manila, a Polish village and a Texas strip mall. Different music, same shape. And the creed says: one, holy, catholic and apostolic.

20.title: prayer like a friendship
20.told: a story of Saint Teresa of Ávila

shots.cap: In the walled Spanish city of Ávila, a girl named Teresa loved stories of saints and knights. At about seven, she and her brother ran away to become martyrs.
An uncle met them just outside the city and brought them home. So they built little hermit huts in the garden instead. The stones kept falling down.
Grown up, Teresa became a Carmelite nun. Yet for years, she admitted, prayer was dry. She would listen for the clock, wishing the hour were over.
Slowly, something changed. She wrote that prayer is simply friendship: taking time, often, to be alone with the one we know loves us.
She was funny and blunt. To nuns stuck with kitchen work, she wrote that God walks among the pots and pans.
People love one story: her cart tipped her into a muddy river, and she told God, “If this is how you treat your friends, no wonder you have so few!”

21.title: one hundred and fifty doors
21.told: from the first book of Samuel

shots.cap: Near Bethlehem, a shepherd boy named David spent long days in the hills with his father’s sheep, and a lyre, a small harp, to pass the time.
In the palace, King Saul was troubled. A dark spirit hung over him, and he could find no peace. His servants had an idea: music.
So David came to the palace. Whenever the darkness came over Saul, David took his harp and played, and Saul was refreshed.
Tradition remembers David as Israel’s great singer. Many of the 150 Psalms carry his name: songs of joy, of anger, of fear, of thanks.
One of the most loved starts with a shepherd, like David once was: “The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want.”
Today, the Church still prays the Psalms every day. A psalm is prayed at Mass, and monks, nuns and priests pray them through the hours of the day.
After the angel left, Mary hurried into the hill country to see her cousin Elizabeth. Elizabeth was old, and expecting a baby too.
Mary came in and greeted her. The moment Elizabeth heard Mary’s hello, the baby inside her leaped.
Filled with the Holy Spirit, Elizabeth cried out, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!”
“Why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord comes to me?” Mary answered with a song of praise, and stayed about three months.
Today, Catholics join the two greetings, the angel’s and Elizabeth’s, into one prayer: the Hail Mary. Then they add a request: pray for us.

24.title: the man who never says a word

shots.cap: In Nazareth lived Joseph, a carpenter from the family of King David. He was promised in marriage to a young woman named Mary.
Then the news: Mary was expecting a child, and the child wasn’t his. In all four Gospels, Joseph never says a single word.
Joseph was a just man. The law gave him harsher options. He chose the gentlest: to end the engagement quietly, so Mary would not be shamed.
An angel came to him in a dream. “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife. The child is from the Holy Spirit.”
Joseph woke up and did exactly what the angel said. He took Mary into his home. No speech. He just did it.
Today, Catholics honor Joseph as patron of the whole Church. Workers, fathers and families ask for his prayers, especially on March 19 and May 1.

25.title: no room
25.told: from Luke’s Gospel and a story of Saint Francis

shots.cap: The emperor ordered everyone counted, so Joseph took Mary, very pregnant, on the long road to Bethlehem, the town of King David.
Every guest room was full. When the baby came, Mary wrapped him in cloth and laid him in a manger, a feeding trough for animals.
Christmas 1223, in the Italian town of Greccio. Francis had a friend set up a manger with hay, an ox and a donkey, in a rocky spot in the woods.
People climbed the hill at night with candles and torches. The woods rang with their songs. Mass was said right there, over the manger.
Francis sang the Gospel and preached about “the baby of Bethlehem” with such tenderness that people never forgot it.
Today, Catholic churches and homes all over the world set up a crib scene at Christmas. Tradition traces the custom to that night at Greccio.

26.title: good news for the night shift

shots.cap: That same night, in the fields outside Bethlehem, shepherds were keeping watch over their flock. The night shift, while the town slept.
Suddenly an angel stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone all around. They were terrified.
“Do not be afraid. I bring you good news of great joy for all the people. Today a Savior is born. You’ll find a baby lying in a manger.”
Then the sky filled with angels, singing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”
The shepherds hurried into Bethlehem and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the manger, just as they’d been told.
They told everyone what they’d heard, and people were amazed. But Mary kept all these things, pondering them in her heart.
Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph carried the baby to the Temple in Jerusalem with two small birds, the offering of families who couldn’t afford a lamb.
In Jerusalem lived a devout man named Simeon. God had promised he would not die before he saw the Messiah. So he waited, day after day.
He came into the Temple courts, saw one more young couple in the crowd, and took their baby in his arms. Then he prayed.
He called the child “a light for the nations, and the glory of your people Israel.” Then, gently, he told Mary a sword would pierce her own soul.
Then came Anna, a prophetess, a widow in her eighties who never left the Temple, praying night and day. She thanked God and spoke of the child to everyone.
Today, on February 2, Catholics bless candles and carry them in procession, because Simeon called the child a light. Many call it Candlemas.
Far to the east, magi, wise men who studied the stars, saw a new star rise. They packed their treasures and set out across the desert to follow it.
In Jerusalem they asked, “Where is the newborn king of the Jews? We saw his star, and we’ve come to worship him.” King Herod was troubled.
The star stopped over a house in Bethlehem. They saw the child with Mary his mother, knelt, and opened their treasures: gold, frankincense and myrrh.
Warned in a dream not to go back to Herod, they went home by another road.
Then Joseph dreamed again: “Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee.” They left that very night, across a border, as refugees.
Today, at Epiphany, some Catholic families chalk the year over the front door with C, M and B: the magi’s old names, and “Christ bless this house” in Latin.

8.title: the man who argued with god

shots.cap: In the heat of the day, an old man named Abraham sat at the door of his tent. Three strangers appeared on the road.
He ran to meet them and fed them: fresh bread, a tender calf, curds and milk. He stood by them under the tree while they ate.
As the guests left, Abraham walked with them, looking down toward Sodom. Then God told him: the outcry against that city is great. I will go and see.
Abraham came closer. “Will you sweep away the righteous with the wicked? Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?”
“What if there are fifty good people in the city?” And God said: for fifty, I will spare the whole place.
So Abraham kept going: forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, calling himself “but dust and ashes.” He stopped at ten. For ten, God said, I will not destroy it.
Today, many Jews still speak up for people who aren’t in the room. Arguing for justice, even with heaven, is part of the tradition.
Twenty years earlier, Jacob had tricked his twin brother Esau out of their father’s blessing, and run. Now he was coming home. Esau was coming too, with four hundred men.
That night, Jacob sent his family and everything he had across the river Jabbok. He stayed behind, alone, in the dark.
And a man wrestled with him until the break of dawn. No name. No warning. Just the two of them in the dust, all night long.
As dawn came, the stranger touched Jacob’s hip and wrenched it. “Let me go,” he said. Jacob answered, “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.”
The blessing was a new name. “No more Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
Jacob named the place Peniel, “the face of God.” The sun rose as he crossed over, and he was limping. Hurt, and renamed, in the same morning.
Today, the Jewish people are still called the children of Israel: named for a man who wrestled all night, and held on.

10.title: we will do, and we will hear

shots.cap: In the third month after Egypt, the freed slaves camped at the foot of a desert mountain called Sinai. They were told to wash, to wait, and to keep back.
On the third morning came thunder and lightning, a thick cloud on the mountain, and the sound of a horn growing louder and louder. The whole camp trembled.
Moses climbed up into the cloud and came down again. Then, the Torah says, God spoke the Ten Commandments from the mountain, to the whole people.
Moses read it all aloud, and the people answered together: “All that the Lord has spoken, we will do, and we will hear.” In Hebrew: na’aseh v’nishma.
The rabbis tell that angels tied two crowns on each person, one for each word. And a voice from heaven asked, “Who revealed to my children the angels’ secret?”
Today, Jews remember that day every spring, at the festival of Shavuot. Many stay up all night studying together, until dawn.
The Talmud tells this. A Roman emperor asked Rabbi Yehoshua, “Why does the food you eat on Shabbat smell so wonderful?”
The rabbi smiled. “We have a spice,” he said, “and its name is Shabbat. We put it in the food, and that’s the smell.”
“Give us some!” said the emperor.
“For anyone who keeps Shabbat,” said Rabbi Yehoshua, “it works. For anyone who doesn’t keep Shabbat, it doesn’t.”
The Torah says that on the seventh day God finished the work, and rested. Then God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy.
Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday night. Orthodox Jews don’t drive, cook or use phones. Many other Jews keep it their own way, with candles, a meal and rest.

12.title: the man who ran after peace

shots.cap: The rabbis tell about Aaron, the brother of Moses. Whenever two people had quarreled and stopped speaking, Aaron went quietly to work.
He sat with the first one and said, “Your friend is heartbroken. He keeps saying, ‘How can I face him? I’m the one who wronged him.’”
Then he went to the other one, sat with him, and said the very same thing.
When the two met, they embraced and kissed each other, friends again.
Centuries later, the great teacher Hillel said: “Be like the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace.”
The Hebrew word for peace is shalom. It comes from a root that means whole, complete, nothing missing. Jews say it for hello, for goodbye, and for peace.
Today, many Jews greet each other with “shalom,” and on the day of rest, “Shabbat shalom.” Underneath the hello is an old wish: may you be whole.
The Talmud tells this story. Jacob, the man renamed Israel, was very old, near the end of his life in Egypt. His twelve sons gathered around his bed.
He had one fear. Would his children keep his faith after he was gone? Maybe one of them didn’t believe what he believed.
His sons answered together: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. Just as there is only One in your heart, so in ours.”
And Jacob, at peace, answered softly: “Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever.”
Today, those six words, Shema Yisrael, are said morning and night. Many cover their eyes with one hand, to shut everything else out and just listen.
Some children learn it as their first prayer, at bedtime. And tradition hopes it will be among the last words a person says, just like at Jacob’s bed.

14.title: the woman who prayed in silence

shots.cap: Every year, Hannah went with her family to the sanctuary at Shiloh. She longed for a child and had none. Year after year, she wept and couldn’t eat.
One year, she rose and went to pray alone. She spoke in her heart. Only her lips moved. Her voice could not be heard.
The priest Eli was watching. He saw her lips moving, heard nothing, and decided she was drunk. “Put away your wine,” he told her.
“No, my lord,” Hannah said. “I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink. I poured out my soul before the Lord.”
Eli understood. “Go in peace,” he said, “and may God grant what you asked.”
She went on her way, and ate, and her face was no longer sad. In time, she had a son. She named him Samuel.
Today, the central Jewish prayer, the Amidah, “the standing prayer,” is said in a whisper. The rabbis learned how from Hannah: lips moving, voice low, heart aimed.

15.title: a thank-you before the first bite

shots.cap: The Talmud tells of a rabbi, Ben Zoma. One day he stood high on the steps of the Temple Mount and looked down at a huge, busy crowd.
He said a blessing out loud: “Blessed is the One who created all these people to serve me.”
He explained. The first human had to do it all alone: plow, sow, reap, thresh, grind, sift, knead and bake. Only then could he eat.
“And I get up in the morning,” said Ben Zoma, “and find it all ready for me.” The farmer, the miller, the baker, the weaver. All of them.
He also said: a good guest says, “How much trouble my host took for me!” A bad guest says, “What trouble? I only ate one piece of bread.”
Today, before an apple or a glass of water, many Jews pause to say a short blessing, a bracha. It isn’t said to the food. It’s said to the source.
In Babylonia, a rabbi named Mar Ukba had a poor neighbor. Every day, he slipped four coins into the socket of the man’s door, where no one would see.
One day the poor man thought, “I’ll go and see who is doing this for me.” So he waited by the door.
That day Mar Ukba was late from study, and his wife came with him. As the door opened, they ran and hid inside a baker’s oven, its fire just swept out.
The oven floor was still hot, and Mar Ukba’s feet were burning. His wife said, “Put your feet on mine.” And they waited, together, in the dark.
Centuries later, the great scholar Maimonides ranked tzedakah in eight levels, often pictured as a ladder. Giving in secret, so no one is ashamed, is near the top.
And the top rung, above all the rest? Helping someone so they won’t need help again: a loan, a partnership, a job.
Today, many Jewish homes keep a small tzedakah box on the counter. Coins go in, often before Shabbat, a little at a time.

17.title: the ten who came back afraid

shots.cap: After the escape from Egypt, Moses sent twelve scouts ahead, one from each tribe, to explore the land of Canaan. They walked it for forty days.
They came back carrying fruit: pomegranates, figs, and one cluster of grapes so big it took two men and a pole to carry it.
But ten of them said the cities were walled and the people were giants. “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.”
That night, the whole people wept. Only two, Joshua and Caleb, stood up and said, “The land is an exceeding good land.”
Later in the story, God calls those ten “this evil congregation.” The rabbis noticed: ten people were called a congregation. So ten became the smallest community in Jewish law.
Today, some prayers need a minyan of ten, like the reading from the Torah scroll and the mourner’s Kaddish. A mourner doesn’t say it alone. Nine others come.
Who counts differs. In Orthodox communities, a minyan is ten men, thirteen and older. In Reform, Reconstructionist and egalitarian Conservative ones, women count equally.
God sent the prophet Jonah to Nineveh, a huge and violent city. Jonah ran the other way, onto a ship, and into the sea. But in the end, he went.
He walked into the city and cried out one short warning: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!”
The people believed. They called a fast and put on sackcloth, rough cloth worn for mourning, from the greatest of them to the least.
Even the king rose from his throne, took off his robe, and sat in ashes. “Who knows?” he said. “God may yet turn, and we will not perish.”
And God saw what they did, that they turned from their evil ways. And the disaster never came.
Today, on Yom Kippur afternoon, the book of Jonah is read aloud. The whole community fasts together and says sorry in the plural: not “I have sinned,” but “we have.”
The Talmud tells of Rabbi Yochanan, a great scholar, famous for his beauty. One day he was bathing in the Jordan River.
A bandit named Reish Lakish saw him and, in one great leap, jumped into the river after him.
Rabbi Yochanan looked at him and said, “Your strength should be for Torah.” Reish Lakish shot back, “Your beauty should be for women!”
“If you turn around,” said the rabbi, “I’ll give you my sister in marriage, and she is more beautiful than I am.” Reish Lakish agreed.
He tried to go back for his things, and couldn’t. Rabbi Yochanan taught him, and he became one of the great sages of his time.
Later, Reish Lakish himself taught: when a person turns back out of love, even their worst wrongs become merits.
Today, the month before the Jewish new year, and the ten days up to Yom Kippur, are set aside for teshuvah. But the door stays open any day.

21.title: the day the scroll was read aloud

shots.cap: Long ago, after years in exile, the people came home to Jerusalem. One autumn day, they all gathered as one, in the square before the Water Gate.
Ezra the scribe climbed onto a tall wooden platform and opened the scroll in front of everyone. When he opened it, all the people stood up.
He read from early morning until midday. Men and women, and everyone old enough to understand, listened.
As he read, the Levites, the teachers, stood among the people. They read clearly, and gave the sense, so the people understood the reading.
The people began to weep. But they were told: don’t grieve. Go, eat rich food, drink something sweet, and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready.
Today, one portion of the Torah, a parsha, is read every Shabbat, with shorter readings on Monday and Thursday mornings. The rabbis credited Ezra with shaping them.
Communities read it in different ways. Orthodox synagogues read the full portion each week. Many Reform and some Conservative ones read part of it, on a three-year cycle.
The Torah opens with its first word, Bereshit: in the beginning. There was darkness over the deep, and the spirit of God hovering over the water.
Then God speaks, and that is all it takes. “Let there be light.” And there was light.
“And there was evening and there was morning, one day.” Not “the first day.” One day.
The rabbis tell a story. The Torah begins with bet, the second letter. So alef, the first letter, came to God and complained, for twenty-six generations.
God said: when I give the Torah at Sinai, I’ll begin with you. And the words spoken at Sinai begin with alef: Anochi, “I am.”
Today, Bereshit is read every autumn, right after the scroll is rolled back to the beginning. In this story, the world is made with words.
In the Torah’s six days: light, then sky, then land and plants. Then sun, moon and stars. Then fish and birds. Then animals, and people.
Again and again, the story says, “And God saw that it was good.” At the end of the sixth day: “Behold, it was very good.”
But the rabbis noticed a puzzle. Light on day one, but no sun until day four. So what was that first light?
The Talmud says it was a special light. By it, the first human could see from one end of the world to the other.
But God saw that later generations would do great harm. So God hid the light away, saved for the righteous in the time to come.
Today, some Jewish teachers say a glimpse of that hidden light can still be found: in study, in kindness, in a moment that is simply good.
You met the great teacher Hillel before. One day, as his class ended, he set off walking, and his students walked with him.
“Rabbi, where are you going?” “To do a mitzvah,” he said, a holy deed. “Which one?” they asked.
“To bathe in the bathhouse,” said Hillel. His students stared. “That’s a mitzvah?”
“Yes,” he said. “The statues of kings in the theaters: someone is paid to scrub and wash them, and is honored for it.”
“How much more must I care for myself, since I was created in the image of God.”
The rabbis said it another way. A king stamps many coins with one seal, and they all look alike. God stamps every person with one seal, and not one is like another.
Today, the same old teaching about the coins is famous for one more line: whoever saves one life, it is as if they saved a whole world.

25.title: the day the bread didn’t fall

shots.cap: In the desert after Egypt, the freed slaves were hungry. “In Egypt, we ate bread until we were full,” they grumbled.
So each morning, when the dew lifted, the ground was covered with something fine and white, like frost. “What is it?” they asked. In Hebrew, man hu. Manna.
Everyone gathered what they needed for the day. Some gathered more, some less, and yet no one had too much, and no one had too little.
On the sixth day, there was twice as much. Moses told them: tomorrow is a day of rest, a holy Shabbat. Bake what you need today.
On the seventh day, some went out anyway with their baskets. They found nothing. So the people rested on the seventh day.
Today, many Jewish families set two loaves of challah on the Shabbat table, under a cloth. Two loaves, for the double bread before that first rest.
In the Torah, God forms the first human from the dust of the ground. The ground is adamah. The human made from it is adam: the earthling.
Then God breathes into his nostrils the breath of life, “and man became a living soul.” Earth and breath, in one person.
In Poland, about two hundred years ago, a Hasidic teacher, Rabbi Simcha Bunim, told his students: everyone should have two pockets.
One slip says, “For my sake the world was created,” a saying of the rabbis. The other has Abraham’s words: “I am but dust and ashes.”
When you feel too proud, reach for the dust. When you feel worthless, reach for the other pocket. The trick, he said, is knowing which one.
Today, some people really do carry two slips of paper, one in each pocket. Earth and breath, both true of you, all the time.

27.title: the man who slept seventy years

shots.cap: The Talmud tells of Honi, a holy man. One day he saw an old man planting a carob tree. “How long until it gives fruit?” he asked. “Seventy years.”
“Will you live seventy years?” The old man said, “I found carob trees in the world. As my ancestors planted for me, I plant for my children.”
Honi sat down to eat, and sleep came over him. Rocks rose up around him, hiding him from view, and he slept for seventy years.
When he woke, a man was picking carobs from the tree. “Did you plant this?” Honi asked. “No, my grandfather did.”
Honi went to the study hall. He heard the scholars say, “These teachings are as clear as in the days of Honi.” “I am Honi!” he said. No one believed him.
Heartbroken, Honi prayed for mercy, and his life came to an end. That, the Talmud says, is the old saying: either friendship, or death.
Today, Jews often study in pairs. A study partner is a chavruta, the very word in Honi’s saying. You learn together, out loud, arguing and laughing.
In the garden, the first man and woman ate from the one tree they were told to leave alone. The text never says apple. Just fruit.
Their eyes were opened. They sewed fig leaves together, and when they heard God in the garden in the cool of the day, they hid among the trees.
And God called to the man, “Where art thou?” In Hebrew, it’s one word: ayekah.
“I heard Thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid,” he said. Then he pointed: the woman gave me the fruit. And she pointed at the snake.
Long after, in a Russian prison, an official asked a jailed rabbi, Shneur Zalman: “If God knows everything, why ask Adam where he is?”
The rabbi answered: in every age, God calls to every person, “Where are you in your world? So many years of your life have passed. Where are you?”
Today, many Jews hear ayekah not as a trap but as a door left open: come out, and say where you are.

8.title: the greeting that is a wish
8.told: a saying of the Prophet ﷺ

shots.cap: A saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells that when God created Adam, the first human, He said to him: go and greet that gathering of angels.
“Listen to how they answer you,” God told him. “That will be your greeting, and your children’s greeting.”
Adam said, “As-salamu alaykum,” peace be upon you. The angels answered, “Peace be upon you, and the mercy of God.”
The Qur’an makes it a rule: when someone greets you, answer with something better, or at least give the same back.
The Prophet ﷺ told his companions: you won’t truly believe until you love one another. And what grows that love? Spread salaam among yourselves.
Today, at a shop or an airport gate, one says, “As-salamu alaykum.” The other answers straight back, “Wa alaykum as-salam.” And upon you, peace.

9.title: a house built on five
9.told: a saying of the Prophet ﷺ

shots.cap: ‘Umar remembered a day in Medina, sitting with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, when a stranger walked in, his clothes brilliant white, his hair very black.
There was no dust of travel on him, yet no one knew him. He sat knee to knee with the Prophet ﷺ and asked, “Tell me about Islam.”
Bear witness that there is no god but God and Muhammad is His messenger. Pray. Give zakat. Fast Ramadan. Make the pilgrimage, if you are able.
“You have spoken truly,” the stranger said. And the companions sitting there were amazed.
He asked about faith, and about worshipping God as if you see Him, then left. It was the angel Jibril, the Prophet ﷺ said, come to teach them their religion.
Another saying puts it in one picture: Islam is built on five. Like a house, held up by its pillars.
Today the five keep different clocks. The witness, always. Prayer, every day. Zakat and the fast, every year. The pilgrimage, once in a life.

10.title: fifty, then five
10.told: a saying of the Prophet ﷺ

shots.cap: One night, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells, he was taken from Mecca to Jerusalem, and from there up through the heavens.
There, God gave him a gift for his people: fifty prayers, every day.
On his way back he met Musa, Moses. “Your people can’t manage that,” Musa told him. “Go back and ask for less.”
He went back, and the number came down. Musa sent him again, and again, until it was five.
“They are five,” God said, “and they are fifty.” Five prayers a day, with the reward of fifty.
The five follow the sun: Fajr before sunrise, Dhuhr after midday, Asr in the afternoon, Maghrib after sunset, Isha at night.
Today, in a stockroom at lunch, a man stands, bows, then sets his forehead on a flattened box. A saying teaches: here, a person is nearest to God.
One day, two men were sitting near the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Then both of them sneezed.
To one he said, “Yarhamuk Allah,” may God have mercy on you. To the other, nothing. The other man asked him why.
“This one praised God,” he said, “and you didn’t.” The first man had said “alhamdulillah”: the praise belongs to God.
Another saying made it a habit: sneeze, say alhamdulillah, and whoever hears you answers, “yarhamuk Allah.” Muslims still do it, at work and at home.
Hamd, praise, isn’t quite shukr, thanks. Thanks answers a good thing done for you. Praise answers who someone is, on any kind of day.
The Prophet ﷺ said the believer’s life is a wonder. When good comes, they’re grateful. When hardship comes, they’re patient. Both are good for them.
Today, ask a grandmother about her terrible knees, and you may hear it first: alhamdulillah. Not pretending. Praise, whatever the day did.

12.title: a drink for a thirsty dog
12.told: a story the Prophet ﷺ told

shots.cap: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once told of a man walking a desert road. He grew so thirsty that he climbed down into a well and drank.
When he climbed out, he saw a dog, panting, licking the damp earth because it was so thirsty.
“This dog is as thirsty as I was,” he thought. He climbed down again, filled his leather sock, held it in his teeth, and climbed up.
He gave the dog water. And God thanked him for it, the Prophet ﷺ said, and forgave him.
“Is there reward for us even with animals?” the companions asked. “In every living thing,” he said, “there is reward.”
Every prayer says it: “Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.” Rabb, Lord, is the one who raises and tends. Worlds, plural: people, animals, everything.
Today, in a summer heat wave, a shopkeeper sets a bowl of water by her door. For whoever comes: a cat, a dog, a sparrow.
One day, captives were brought before the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Among them, a mother was rushing from child to child, searching.
Whenever she found a baby among them, she pulled it close to her and fed it.
The Prophet ﷺ turned to his companions. “Could this woman ever throw her own child into a fire?” “No,” they said, “not if she could help it.”
“God is more merciful to His servants,” he said, “than this mother is to her child.”
Another saying: God made mercy in a hundred parts, and sent one part into the world. With it, a mare lifts her hoof so she won’t hurt her foal.
And when God finished creating, a saying tells, He wrote in a book kept with Him: “My mercy outstrips My anger.”
Today, every prayer says two names right after “Lord of the worlds”: ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim. Both come from r-h-m, mercy, the root of the Arabic word for womb.

14.title: the merchant who let it go
14.told: a story the Prophet ﷺ told

shots.cap: The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told of a merchant, long ago, who lent money to people. When a debt came due and someone couldn’t pay, he did something unusual.
“Let it go,” he told his helpers. “Maybe God will let us go too.”
When his account was called, a saying tells, nothing good was found in it, except this one habit of letting debts go.
And God said, “I am more worthy of letting go than he is. Let him go.”
Every prayer, right after the two names of mercy, says: “Owner of the Day of Judgment.” Din means repayment, what each is due. Its root also gives dayn, debt.
And nothing quiet is lost. A saying teaches: a good deed you meant to do, even one you never got to, is written down as a whole good deed.
And a wrong you meant to do, then let go of for God’s sake, is written as a good deed too. The angry text, deleted before it was sent.
In Mecca’s early years, a man named Bilal was enslaved. He had become a Muslim, and the man who owned him wanted him to take it back.
The early biographies say he was made to lie on the hot sand at noon, with a heavy rock placed on his chest. “Give it up,” they told him.
He said only one word, again and again. “Ahad. Ahad.” One. One. Later, Abu Bakr, a friend of the Prophet ﷺ, bought him and set him free.
His word sits inside the prayer too. After four lines about God, al-Fatiha turns and speaks to Him: “You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help.”
In the Arabic, “You” comes first: iyyaka na‘budu, You we worship. Putting it first means only You. The word for that is tawhid, making one.
Today, a phone buzzes, the inbox fills, a worry tugs. Tawhid says all of it is real, and none of it is God. One center, instead of a dozen.

16.title: a line in the sand
16.told: a saying of the Prophet ﷺ

shots.cap: A companion named Ibn Mas‘ud remembered a day when the Prophet ﷺ sat with them and began to draw in the sand.
First he drew one straight line. “This is the path of God,” he said.
Then lines to the right and left. “These are paths,” he said, “and on each one is a shaytan, a tempter, calling to it.”
Then he recited from the Qur’an: “This is My straight path, so follow it, and don’t follow other ways, or they will scatter you.”
Al-Fatiha asks for exactly this: “Show us the straight path, the path of those You have blessed.” A road with footprints already on it.
Ihdina, show us, guide us, comes from the root h-d-y. The same root gives hadiya, a gift. Guidance is something handed to you.
Today, lost in a strange city, phone at two percent, you finally stop someone and ask: which way? Al-Fatiha asks that in every prayer.
When the Muslims first came to Medina, there was no call to prayer. People gathered by guessing the time.
So they talked it over. Ring a bell, as the Christians did? Blow a horn, as the Jews did? Light a fire?
‘Abdullah ibn Zayd dreamed of a man carrying a bell. Instead of selling it, the man taught him words: Allahu akbar, God is greatest.
In the morning he told the Prophet ﷺ. “It is a true dream,” he said. “Teach it to Bilal. His voice carries further.”
So Bilal called. The man once held under a rock for saying “one” now called a whole city to the One.
Today, five times a day, the same words rise from city rooftops, one voice a beat behind another, never quite in sync.
And whoever hears the call, a saying teaches, repeats it softly, line by line. Even in a kitchen, from a phone, mid-cup of tea.
One Friday in Medina, the Prophet ﷺ stood giving the weekly sermon, and the mosque was full.
Then a caravan arrived from the north, camels heavy with food, and a sound of drums at the edge of town.
People slipped out, one after another, until only twelve were left with him.
The Qur’an named it: when they see trade or amusement, they rush to it and leave you standing. Say: what is with God is better.
Just before that, the same surah sets the rule: when the Friday call comes, hurry to remember God and leave your trading. Then, after the prayer, go back out.
Today, just after noon on a Friday, a cab driver parks, a nurse swaps a shift, a shopkeeper pulls the shutter halfway. All walking one way.
An hour later they all walk back, and the city picks up where it left off. Jumu‘ah: the gathering day.

19.title: three men and a stranger
19.told: a story the Prophet ﷺ told

shots.cap: The Prophet ﷺ told of three poor men, long ago: one with a skin disease people shrank from, one bald, and one blind.
God sent an angel to test them. Each was healed, and given one animal about to give birth: a camel, a cow, a sheep.
Years passed. The first had a valley full of camels, the second a valley of cows, the third a valley of sheep.
The first two said no. “I have many costs,” they said, and “I inherited all this.” They had forgotten where it came from.
The third said: “I was blind, and God gave me back my sight. Take whatever you want.” “Keep it,” the angel said. “You were only being tested.”
That’s the heart of zakat. Its root, z-k-w, means both to purify and to grow. Like pruning a vine: cut some away, and what’s left grows better.
Today, once a year, a Muslim with savings above a set line, the nisab, gives two and a half percent. Often worked out at a kitchen table, with a pencil.

20.title: the man they called trustworthy
20.told: from the early biographies and the hadith

shots.cap: Long ago in Mecca, the clans rebuilt the Ka‘ba, the old house of worship. When it came to setting the sacred Black Stone back, they nearly came to blows.
Every clan wanted the honor. So, the early biographies say, they agreed: the next man through the gate would decide.
He spread out a cloak, set the stone in the middle, and asked a man from each clan to take a corner. Together they lifted it.
Years later, he climbed the hill of Safa and called the clans together. “If I told you riders in the valley were about to attack you, would you believe me?”
“Yes,” they said. “We have never known you to lie.” Then he gave them his message, and many turned away.
Even so, the early biographies say, many who refused his message still left their valuables in his care. Trusted first. Believed, by many, only later.
Today, someone hands a neighbor the spare key. Not to the most impressive person they know. To the one who has never let them down.
The Prophet ﷺ once sent a man to lead a small expedition. Each time he led their prayer, he ended his recitation the same way.
With one short surah, four lines long: “Say: He is God, the One.” Every single time.
“Ask him why he does it,” the Prophet ﷺ said. The man answered: “Because it describes the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it.”
“Tell him,” the Prophet ﷺ said, “that God loves him.”
It sits near the very end of the Qur’an, in its last thirtieth, juz’ ‘amma, where the short surahs are. That’s where almost everyone starts.
Today, a five-year-old and her grandmother know the same few surahs by heart. Al-Fatiha first, then the short ones, starting from the back.
And three weeks in, you know the words a Muslim day is built from: bismillah, salaam, alhamdulillah, ahad. The foothills, done.
The first story doesn’t start on earth. It starts in a conversation. God tells the angels: “I am placing a steward on the earth.”
The angels ask: “Will You place there one who will cause harm and shed blood, while we praise You?”
God doesn’t scold them. He says only: “I know what you do not know.”
The word is khalifah: one who stands in for another. Not the owner of the garden. The one it’s entrusted to.
A saying puts it plainly: the world is sweet and green, and God has made you stewards in it, to see how you act.
Today, a mother and son plant a sapling in the park. A saying teaches: whatever any creature eats from it counts as charity.
Yesterday the angels asked why. Now God answers, not with an argument, but a test. He sets things before them: “Tell Me their names.”
The angels answer honestly: “Glory be to You. We know nothing except what You have taught us.”
God had taught Adam all the names. “Adam, tell them,” He said. And Adam named them, one by one.
“Didn’t I tell you,” God said, “that I know the hidden things of the heavens and the earth?”
What were the names? The Qur’an doesn’t say. One early scholar said everything, down to a bowl and a cooking pot.
Today, a toddler points. Dog. Ball. Moon. Each word, a small victory. Once a child can say moon, they can ask where it goes in the day.
And grown-ups keep learning names: a bird, a tree, a neighbor’s name you never asked. To name a thing is to notice it.

24.title: the one who would not bow

shots.cap: God told the angels to bow before Adam, the first human. And they bowed, every one of them.
All except Iblis. Elsewhere the Qur’an says he was of the jinn, beings made of fire. “What kept you from bowing?” God asked.
“I am better than him,” Iblis said. “You made me from fire, and him from clay.”
What held him back wasn’t hunger or fear. It was a comparison. Pride, the first wrong in the story.
The Prophet ﷺ defined pride simply: rejecting the truth, and looking down on people.
Today, someone younger is made team lead. A quiet thought arrives fully formed: under them? I’m better than that. It’s a very old thought.
God gave Adam and his wife a home: a garden. “Live in it,” He said, “and eat freely from it, wherever you like.”
The Qur’an describes the garden’s promise: no hunger there, no thirst, no going without clothes, no burning sun.
Then one limit: “Don’t come near this tree, or you will be wrongdoers.” Not even “don’t eat.” Don’t come near.
Notice what the Qur’an doesn’t say. It doesn’t name the tree, or the fruit. It doesn’t even name his wife. Later tradition calls her Hawwa, Eve.
Today, a friend lends you their apartment. Use the car, the books, the good coffee. Just don’t open the hall cupboard. Guess what you think about.
A hundred yeses, and one no. It’s an old joke which one keeps you up the first night.
In the garden, with everything given and one tree held back, someone began to talk. Not with a shout. With a whisper.
“Then Shaytan whispered to them,” the Qur’an says. The Arabic is waswasa. Say it slowly: was-was. The word itself whispers.
He didn’t say “disobey God.” He renamed the tree: the tree of forever, a kingdom that never wears out. And he swore he was their sincere adviser.
They both ate. At once they saw their nakedness, and began covering themselves with leaves of the garden.
Today, at two in the morning, a voice starts up. Reasonable. One more episode. Or: you’ll never be good enough. It sounds exactly like you.
Companions once told the Prophet ﷺ of thoughts too awful to say out loud. “You really find that?” he asked. “That is clear faith.”
After the whisper, Adam and his wife stood in the garden, covered in leaves. And their Lord called to them.
This was their fork in the road. Remember Iblis? When he was sent away, he blamed God: “Because You led me astray.”
They said: “Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves. If You don’t forgive us and have mercy on us, we will be lost.”
Then Adam received words from his Lord, the Qur’an says, and God turned toward him. He is the One who keeps turning, the Merciful.
A saying adds a picture: God is happier at a person’s return than a traveler who lost his camel in the desert, then finds it standing right there.
Today, a mistake lands, and it’s clearly yours. One way out: explain. The other: three hard words. I was wrong.
Now the story comes down to earth, and the first thing it shows is a family. Two sons of Adam each bring an offering to God.
One offering is accepted. The other isn’t. And the brother whose offering was refused says: “I will kill you.”
His brother answers: “God accepts only from the mindful. Even if you raise your hand to kill me, I won’t raise mine to kill you.”
The Qur’an says simply: his soul talked him into it, and he took his brother’s life. Then God sent a crow, scratching gently at the earth.
Watching it, he learned how to lay his brother in the earth. “Woe is me!” he cried. “Couldn’t I even be like this crow?” And he was full of regret.
Right after, the Qur’an draws its lesson: whoever wrongly takes one life, it is as if they killed all people. Whoever saves one, as if they saved all.
Today, a woman in a first-aid class practices chest compressions on a dummy. One life saved, the Qur’an says, is like saving everyone.

Rama’s army said it was a trap. But Rama said: anyone who comes to me even once asking for shelter, I protect.
Vibhishana left everything behind for what was right. And he was welcomed into a whole new life.

1.told: a story from the Pali Canon

shots.cap: a monk bows to everyone he meets.

people get angry. who is this fool?
they throw stones. he steps back. and says it again.
the buddha said: that monk was me.
today: three bows. buddha, dharma, sangha.
a huge crowd. the most beautiful dancer in the land.
you carry a bowl of oil, full to the brim, right past her.

four truths: the ache. its cause. it can end. a path.
one friend gets it: whatever begins, ends.
the prince who left comes home. as a monk.
he walks the streets with a bowl, house to house.

the king: no one in our family has ever begged!

6.told: as the old texts tell it

shots.cap: a newborn who stood up and walked. that's the story.

7.title: one lamp lights another
7.told: from the Questions of King Milinda

shots.cap: a greek king who loved hard questions.
then he meets a monk named nagasena.
reborn: same person, or someone else?
the flame at midnight: same as the one at dusk?
neither the same, nor another.
