when someone dies, families share good in their name.

8.title: not “suffering”
8.told: a story from the Buddhist commentaries

shots.cap: In the city of Savatthi lived a young mother named Kisa Gotami. When her little son died, she could not accept it.
She went from house to house, asking everyone for medicine to bring him back. People pitied her. Nobody could help.
At last someone sent her to the Buddha. “I know a medicine,” he said gently. “Bring me a handful of mustard seeds.”
“But they must come from a house where no one has ever died.” Glad, she hurried back into the town.
At every door, people gladly held out seeds. Then she asked her question. “The living are few,” they said, “but the dead are many.”
By evening she understood. Not one house was untouched. Her grief was real, and it was not hers alone.
She laid her son to rest and went back to the Buddha, her hands empty. Later she became a nun, remembered as one who woke up.
Today, someone tells a friend what’s been hard. The friend says, “Me too.” Nothing is fixed. But the wobble is shared.
Long ago, an old tale says, lived King Mandhata. At a touch of his hands, jewels rained from the sky, piling up knee-deep.
He ruled the whole earth. He had everything a person could want. Still, something in him leaned toward more.
So he rose to the heavens. There Sakka, king of the gods, welcomed him and shared half his throne.
For ages he ruled half of heaven. Then one thought arrived: “Why only half? I want it all.”
With that thought, his power left him. He fell back to earth, an old man, in his own garden.
Before he died, he told the people: “I had treasure, the earth and half of heaven, and it was never enough.”
Today, a slow line at the store. The jaw tightens. The line isn’t hurting anyone. The wanting it to be different is.

10.title: the lamp that went out
10.told: from the verses of the first Buddhist nuns

shots.cap: Long ago, a woman named Patacara lost her whole family in one terrible stretch of days. Grief nearly broke her mind.
She came to the Buddha with nothing left. “Sister,” he said gently, “come back to yourself.” She stayed, and became a nun.
Years of practice passed. Still she wondered: farmers plough and their fields reward them. Why have I not found peace?
One evening, washing her feet, she watched the water run down the slope. She steadied her mind, the way you’d calm a good horse.
That night she sat by her lamp. With a needle, she drew down the wick.
The flame went out. “Like the lamp going out,” her verse says, “my mind was set free.”
Today, at the end of a long day, a small quiet opens between two thoughts. The third truth points at moments like that.
Once the Buddha told a story. A man was wandering, lost, in a deep forest.
Under the vines he found an old path, worn smooth by feet from long ago. He followed it.
It led to an ancient city, empty for ages: walls, parks, groves and lotus ponds, all waiting under the leaves.
He went to the king and told him what he had found. The king had the city restored.
In time the city was alive again, thriving and full of people.
“Just so,” said the Buddha. “I found an ancient path, walked by awakened ones long before me. It is the eightfold path.”
Today, the path looks like this: a kinder word to your sister, an honest moment at work, one small harm skipped.
In the kingdom of Kosala lived a bandit named Angulimala. He had taken so many lives that whole villages emptied when he came near.
One morning the Buddha walked alone toward his forest. Cowherds begged him, “Turn back! Angulimala is there!” He kept walking, in silence.
Angulimala saw him and ran after him. But however fast he ran, he could not catch a man who was only walking.
“Stop, monk!” he shouted. The Buddha said, “I have stopped, Angulimala. You stop too.”
“How have you stopped, when you’re walking?” “I have stopped harming living beings, for good,” said the Buddha. “You have not.”
Something in Angulimala broke open. He threw his sword into a ravine, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, and asked to become a monk.
Later he blessed a woman in hard labor: “Since my noble birth, I don’t recall ever knowingly taking a life. By this truth, may you both be well.” They were.
Today, many Buddhists recite five lines, at temples and at home: not to harm, steal, misuse sex, lie, or cloud the mind.
The Buddha was eighty. In a grove of sal trees near Kusinara, he lay down between two trees. It would be his last night.
The old texts say the trees burst into bloom out of season, and their flowers drifted down onto him.
His friend Ananda slipped away, leaned on a door post, and wept. “My teacher, who was so kind to me, is leaving.”
The Buddha called him. “Enough, Ananda. Haven’t I taught you? All that is dear to us must change. How could it be otherwise?”
Then he praised Ananda’s long years of loving care. “Keep going,” he said, “and soon you too will be free.”
Near the end, he spoke his last words: “All things that are made pass away. Strive on, with care.”
Today, a leaf in October: green in spring, red and gold now, on the sidewalk next week. The leaf, the mood, the year.
A wandering seeker named Vacchagotta came to the Buddha with a big question. He sat down and asked it straight out.
“Master Gotama,” he said, “is there a self?” A real me, at the center of everything?
The Buddha was silent. “Then is there no self?” Again the Buddha was silent. So Vacchagotta got up and left.
His attendant Ananda was puzzled. “Why didn’t you answer him?”
“If I had said yes,” the Buddha explained, “he would have held on to a fixed self. That wouldn’t fit the truth that nothing can be held as a self.”
“And if I had said no, he was already confused. He would think, ‘I used to have a self, and now it’s gone.’”
Today, say the word “I” and try to point to it. The body has changed. Moods turn twice before lunch. Who’s in there?

15.title: wishing well, even on them
15.told: a story from the Buddhist commentaries

shots.cap: Long ago, a group of monks went deep into a forest to spend the rainy season meditating at the foot of its great trees.
But the tree spirits who lived there didn’t want them. At night they sent frightening shapes, strange sounds and foul smells to drive the monks away.
Shaking, the monks told the Buddha everything. “Go back to the same forest,” he said. “This time, take protection with you.”
The protection was a teaching on metta, friendliness. Wish every being well, he said, the way a mother guards her only child.
The monks walked back chanting it, wishing even the spirits well. The spirits felt it. They softened, and began to watch over the monks instead.
Today, the coworker who replies all. Metta doesn’t ask you to like them, or to agree. Just: may you be at ease.
One day the Buddha and Ananda were walking past the monks’ huts. In one, a monk lay sick on the floor, too weak to get up, all alone.
“Why isn’t anyone caring for you?” the Buddha asked. “I’m no use to the other monks,” he said. “So nobody looks after me.”
The Buddha sent Ananda for water. The Buddha poured, Ananda washed, and together they lifted the monk gently onto a bed.
Then he called all the monks together. “You have no mother or father here to care for you. If you don’t care for each other, who will?”
“Whoever would care for me,” he said, “let them care for the sick.”
Today, a friend’s quiet kitchen after bad news. Compassion doesn’t rush to fix it. It sits down beside them, and stays.
Three monks lived together in a quiet forest grove. One day the Buddha came to visit, and asked one of them, Anuruddha, how they were getting on.
“Do you live in harmony,” he asked, “blending like milk and water, looking at each other with kind eyes?”
“I think, how lucky I am to live with friends like these,” Anuruddha said. “So I set aside what I want, and do what they want.”
Whoever saw the water pot empty filled it. If it was too heavy, he waved a friend over, and they lifted it together, without a word.
And every fifth night they sat up together, talking about the teaching. “We are different in body,” Anuruddha said, “but one in mind.”
Today, a shared kitchen. Somebody always refills the water jug, and nobody sees who. In the old word, that small refill is sangha.
In a tale of the Buddha’s past lives, he was once a monkey king, leading his troop in a great mango tree beside the river Ganges.
One night a human king, who loved the tree’s mangoes, surrounded it with archers. At dawn, they would shoot.
The monkey king leapt across the river, tied a long cane to a tree on the far bank, tied the other end to his waist, and leapt back.
But the cane was too short. So he grabbed a branch and stretched his own body across the gap. “Cross,” he told them. “Over my back.”
One by one, the whole troop ran over him to safety. He held on, though he was hurt and worn out.
The watching human king was moved. He had the monkey king gently brought down, and the dying monkey taught him how a king cares for his people.
Today, someone stays late so a friend can make the deadline. A small bridge. It costs something, and it holds.
A well-known Zen story tells of Hakuin, a teacher in a Japanese village, praised by all his neighbors as a man who lived a pure life.
Then a young woman nearby found she was expecting a baby. Pressed by her angry parents, she named Hakuin as the father. They stormed to his door.
Hakuin listened, and said only, “Is that so?” When the baby was born, they brought the child to him. He took the baby in.
His good name was gone, and people turned away. But he cared for the baby tenderly, asking neighbors for the milk it needed.
A year later, the young mother told the truth: the father was a young man from the fish market. Her parents hurried back to apologize and take the child home.
Hakuin gently handed back the child. All he said was, “Is that so?”
Today, a glowing review and a harsh comment, in the same hour. The winds still blow. The rock still feels them. It just doesn’t move.
Sona grew up rich and sheltered, with soft, delicate feet. He became a monk, and was determined to wake up fast.
He walked in meditation day and night, pushing so hard his feet grew raw. Still nothing. “Maybe I should go home,” he thought, “and do good with my wealth.”
“Sona,” the Buddha asked, “when you lived at home, weren’t you good at the lute?” “Yes,” said Sona.
“When the strings were too tight, did it play well?” No. “Too loose?” No. “And when they were tuned just right?” “Then it played beautifully.”
“Effort is the same,” the Buddha said. “Too much makes you restless. Too little makes you lazy. Find the tuning.” Sona did, and before long he woke up.
Today, a late night at the desk, shoulders up by the ears. Or a whole weekend lost to the couch. Check your strings.
An old monk named Cakkhupala had lost his sight. Still he kept practicing, walking slowly up and down his path through the night.
It was the rainy season. On the wet path, without knowing it, he stepped on insects that had come out after the rain.
In the morning, visiting monks found them. “Look what he did,” they told the Buddha. “He’s been killing living things.”
“Did you see him kill them?” “No.” “Just as you didn’t see him, he didn’t see them. He meant no harm. Where there’s no intention, there’s no bad karma.”
Then, the story says, the Buddha spoke a verse: the mind leads. Act with a bad mind, and pain follows, like the wheel that follows the ox.
Today, a friend breaks your favorite mug by accident. The mug is gone either way. What they meant still matters.
In the city of Kapilavatthu, Queen Maya, wife of King Suddhodana, lay down to sleep one night in the palace.
She dreamed that four guardian spirits lifted her bed and carried her to the mountains, where she was bathed in a still lake and laid on a heavenly couch.
A white elephant with six tusks came down from a golden mountain, a white lotus in its trunk. It circled her three times, and seemed to enter her right side.
In the morning she told the king. He called the wise men who read signs. “Be glad,” they said. “The queen will have a son.”
“If he stays home, he’ll be a great king who rules the world. If he leaves home, he’ll be a buddha, one who wakes up.”
Today, a couple tapes a first scan photo to the fridge. Before a child is born, people are already dreaming about who they’ll be.
A century or two after the Buddha, India had a great emperor, Ashoka. After a terrible war, he was filled with regret, and turned to the Buddha’s teaching.
Years later, he traveled in person to a small garden called Lumbini, the place where the Buddha had been born.
He bowed there, and had a tall stone pillar set up. Carved on it, in plain words: here the Buddha, the sage of the Sakyas, was born.
He also freed the village of Lumbini from most of its taxes. It would pay only an eighth share of its harvest. A gift, for the place he was born.
Over the centuries, the jungle grew back and the place was nearly forgotten. In 1896, the pillar was found again, its words still readable.
Today, pilgrims from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Tibet, Japan and far beyond walk through Lumbini’s gardens, past Ashoka’s pillar, to the place he was born.
High in the mountains lived an old sage named Asita. One day, the story says, he saw the gods celebrating. “A child is born,” they said, “who will wake up.”
Asita hurried down to the palace. The Sakyans showed him the baby prince, and the old man took him in his arms.
He looked closely, the way an expert looks at something rare, and his face lit up. “This one is supreme,” he said, “the highest among people.”
The family was frightened. “Is the child in danger?” “No,” said Asita. “I weep for myself. I am old. I’ll be gone before he teaches, and never hear it.”
So he went to his young nephew, Nalaka. “When you hear that someone has woken up and is teaching,” he said, “go to him.” Years later, Nalaka did.
Today, an old woman plants a tree whose shade she won’t sit in. A teacher believes in a kid she won’t see grown.
Seven days after the prince was born, his mother, Queen Maya, died. Her younger sister, Mahapajapati, took the baby into her arms.
She had a newborn son of her own. The commentaries say she gave him to nurses, and nursed the prince herself, raising him as her own.
Years later, after he had become the Buddha, she spun and wove a new cloth herself, and brought it to him. “Please accept this from me.”
“Give it to the community, Gotami,” he said. “Then it honors me and them both.” She asked three times. Three times he said the same.
Then Ananda spoke up for her. “She is his mother’s sister, his nurse, his foster mother. She fed him when his own mother died.”
Later, she asked to become a nun. It took asking more than once, and Ananda’s help again, but she became the first Buddhist nun.
Today, a grandmother does the school run. A stepdad learns to braid hair. Love can be adopted, and it counts.
Five days after the prince was born, the king held a naming feast. Learned brahmins came to the palace, and eight were asked to read the baby’s marks.
Seven of them raised two fingers. “Two roads,” they said. “If he stays home, a great king. If he leaves home, a buddha.”
The youngest, Kondanna, raised just one. “There is only one road for him,” he said. “He will leave home, and become a buddha.”
They named the boy Siddhattha: the one whose aim succeeds. Siddha means accomplished. Attha means aim, or purpose.
Remember the five friends in the deer park? The story says Kondanna was one of them, and years later, the very first to understand the Buddha’s teaching.
Today, a parent whispers a newborn’s name for the first time. Every name carries a wish someone made for you.
In the later tellings, the king held a royal plowing festival. He guided the first plow himself, and the whole town came out to watch.
The little prince was left on a couch in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree. His nurses slipped away to see the festival.
Alone, the boy sat cross-legged, and his mind grew still. A quiet joy came, the texts say, apart from wanting anything at all.
Hours later the nurses ran back. The sun had moved, but the tree’s shadow had stayed over him. The king, seeing it, bowed to his own son.
Years later, worn thin by harsh fasting, the Buddha-to-be remembered that day. “Could that be the way to awakening?” he wondered. And he knew it was.
Today, a quiet corner, a window seat, a bench in the shade. A small ease shows up. You don’t have to be afraid of it.

28.title: whose swan?
28.told: a later telling of the Buddha’s life

shots.cap: Here’s a much-loved later telling. Young Siddhattha was walking in the palace gardens when a flock of swans flew overhead.
His cousin Devadatta drew his bow and shot. One swan tumbled from the sky, an arrow in its wing, and came down near the prince.
Siddhattha got there first. He knelt, gently drew out the arrow, and held the bird close to calm it.
So they took it to the wise men of the court. “I brought it down,” said Devadatta. “I kept it alive,” said Siddhattha.
The court said: a life belongs to the one who saves it, not the one who tries to take it. The prince nursed the swan, then let it fly.
Today, a kid carries a stunned bird to a shoebox lined with soft towels. Small hands, the same choice.
his dad hid pain from him.
a white parasol, day and night.
one for the cold, one for the hot, one for the rains.
"i was delicately nurtured."
no reason to look past the garden wall.
comfort can be a wall.
she's not his trophy.
yasodhara: she who bears glory.
born on the same day as him.
together across many past lives.
later, a nun in her own right.
partner, not prize.

1.title: the lamps of the sky
1.told: a sakhi, a traditional story of Guru Nanak

shots.cap: guru nanak and his muslim friend mardana walk to a temple by the sea.
at dusk, priests wave golden trays of lamps.
guru nanak doesn't join in. why?
he points up. the sky is the tray. the stars are the pearls.
the whole world is already doing aarti.
bigger than words? waheguru: wow, the teacher.

2.title: the emperor on the floor
2.told: a traditional story of Guru Amar Das and Emperor Akbar

shots.cap: a kitchen where everyone eats on the floor, in rows.
then the most powerful man in india shows up.
the rule: sit in the row first. so the emperor sits with farmers.
he offers land. the guru says no.
the kitchen runs on ordinary people's hands.
every gurdwara is open to anyone. cover your head. come in.

3.title: a crown you tie yourself
3.told: a sakhi from Guru Gobind Singh’s childhood

shots.cap: a kid throws gold into the river. on purpose.
his gold bangle, gone into the ganges.
his mother: where did it fall? show me.
so he throws the other one. right there.
turbans were for kings. he gave every sikh a crown.
uncut hair. a turban tied fresh each morning. a plain steel kara.

4.title: five who said yes
4.told: the history and tradition of Vaisakhi, 1699

shots.cap: 1699. a huge crowd. the guru raises a sword.
who will give their head? silence. then one man stands.
into the tent. the guru comes out alone.
four more stand. a farmer, a water-carrier, a printer, a barber.
all five walk out alive. the five beloved.
then the guru asks the five to give him amrit too.
every vaisakhi, five walk at the front.

5.title: water for both sides
5.told: a sakhi of Bhai Ghanaiya, a traditional story

shots.cap: a battlefield. the wounded lie on both sides.
an old sikh walks among them with a water bag.
he gives water to everyone. the enemy too.
he's helping the enemy!
i don't see friend or enemy. i see you in every face.
the guru gives him balm: ease their wounds too.
sarbat da bhala. the good of all.

6.title: out of the river
6.told: a sakhi, a traditional story of Guru Nanak

shots.cap: he walks into the river. he doesn't come out.
three days. the town searches the banks.
then he walks out: there is no hindu, there is no muslim.
the judge says: then come pray with us.
in the mosque, he doesn't bow.
your mind was at home with your new foal. the judge goes quiet.
sikh means learner. a faith of its own.

7.title: two swords, one circle
7.told: a sakhi of Guru Hargobind, a traditional story

shots.cap: a young guru asks for not one sword. two.
one for the world. one for the spirit.
a famous holy man stops him in the hills.
why ride with swords and horses?
inside, a hermit. outside, a prince.
two swords wrap the khanda, on the sikh flag.
a circle with no end, like the one god.

8.title: the hands nobody sees
8.told: a sakhi of Guru Amar Das, a traditional story

shots.cap: Long ago, an old man named Amar Das walked to the river every morning before dawn, to fill a pitcher of water for his teacher, Guru Angad.
He carried it a long way back to the village of Khadur, so the Guru could bathe. He did it for years, and never asked for thanks.
One stormy night, in the dark and the rain, he tripped beside a weaver’s hut and fell. He kept hold of the pitcher.
Inside, the weaver’s wife grumbled: that must be Amru nithaavan, homeless old Amru, with no place of his own.
Guru Angad said: he is not homeless. He is the home of the homeless. In time, he chose Amar Das as the third Guru.
Today, in gurdwaras everywhere, people still serve like this: shoes handed back, plates scrubbed, roti rolled by someone you’ll never meet.
Sikhs call it seva, selfless service, and name three kinds: with your body, with your mind, and with what you have.
before any story, any rule: a number.
it starts with a numeral: one.
a line with no end.
onkar: a very old sound for the divine.
there is one.
one.

10.title: shiny on the outside
10.told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

shots.cap: On one of his journeys, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana stopped at a roadside inn run by a man named Sajjan.
Sajjan seemed so holy. He had built a temple for his Hindu guests and a mosque for his Muslim guests, and welcomed every traveler.
But at night, while his guests slept, Sajjan robbed them. His holiness was a mask.
That night, Guru Nanak asked Mardana to play, and he sang. Sajjan, waiting in the dark, stopped to listen.
The song said: bronze is bright and shiny, but rub it, and its blackness shows. Wash it a hundred times, and it still won’t come clean.
Sajjan knew the song was about him. He fell at the Guru’s feet, told the truth, and gave what he had stolen to the poor.
At the top of the Sikh scripture, God is called Sat Naam: truth is the name. Sat means what really is, not what shines.

11.title: the boulder on the hill
11.told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

shots.cap: On a blazing day in the hills, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana were walking. Mardana was desperately thirsty, and there was no water anywhere.
At the top of the hill, beside the only spring, sat a Sufi holy man, Wali Qandhari. Mardana climbed up and asked for a drink.
In this telling, he refused: if your master is so great, let him give you water. Three times Mardana climbed, and three times he was turned away.
The Guru told Mardana to lift a stone at the foot of the hill, and fresh water bubbled up. Up at the top, the old spring began to dry.
The holy man was furious. He pushed a huge boulder down the hill, straight at them.
Guru Nanak raised his open hand and stopped it. Many Sikhs say his handprint is still in the rock today.
The Sikh root verse says God is nirbhau, nirvair: without fear, without hate. Sikhs take it as a picture of who a person can become.

12.title: two kinds of bread
12.told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

shots.cap: In the town of Saidpur, Guru Nanak stayed with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter who earned every coin with his own two hands.
Lalo shared what he had: coarse, plain bread. The Guru ate it gladly.
Across town, a rich official, Malik Bhago, threw a great feast for holy men. Everyone came, except Guru Nanak.
Bhago was insulted, and sent for him. Why do you eat a poor man’s bread and refuse mine?
He took Lalo’s bread in one hand and Bhago’s rich food in the other, and squeezed.
From Lalo’s bread came drops of milk. From Bhago’s came drops of blood. His wealth had been squeezed out of the poor.
Sikhs call this kirat karni: honest work. Earn your living by your own effort, without cheating anyone.

13.title: a needle for the next world
13.told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

shots.cap: In Lahore lived a very rich man named Duni Chand. Over his house flew flags, one for every hundred thousand rupees he owned.
When Guru Nanak came to visit, Duni Chand showed him everything, and asked: is there anything I can do for you?
The Guru handed him a small sewing needle. Keep this for me, he said. Give it back to me in the next world.
His wife asked: how will you take a needle with you when you die? Nobody can take anything.
Duni Chand ran back. I can’t carry even a needle, he said. Then how will all your fortune go with you? the Guru asked.
So Duni Chand began to share: food and money for the hungry, given with his own hands.
Sikhs call this vand chakna: share, then eat. Many set aside a tenth of what they earn for others, called dasvandh.

14.title: the pot that stayed cool
14.told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

shots.cap: On their travels, Mardana once wandered off alone into a deep forest, looking for food.
There lived Kauda, a fierce man every traveler feared. He caught Mardana, tied him up, and set a huge pot of oil over the fire to throw him in.
Guru Nanak came into the clearing and began to sing. Tradition says that however high the fire burned, the oil would not boil. It stayed cool.
Kauda fell at the Guru’s feet and wept. He let Mardana go, and changed his ways. The fiercest man in the forest came out a new one.
Remember the river Bein? Sikhs say Guru Nanak came out of it with a charge: remember the Name, and help others remember. In the forest, that’s what he did.

15.title: the congregation
15.told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

shots.cap: On his travels, Guru Nanak and his friend Mardana came to a village where nobody would welcome them. People mocked them and shut their doors.
As they left, the Guru turned and blessed the village: may you stay settled here, always.
At the next village, people ran out to meet them. They fed them, sang hymns with them, and gave them a place to sleep.
As they left, he blessed them: may you be scattered. Mardana stopped in the road. Master, why bless the cruel to stay and the kind to scatter?
The Guru said: let the unkind stay where they are, so their ways don’t spread. Let the good scatter, and carry goodness wherever they go.
Sikhs call it sangat: the company you keep. The stories say that wherever Guru Nanak went, he left a small circle behind, to sing and share food.

16.title: four doors, one number
16.told: the history and tradition of the Harmandir Sahib

shots.cap: Over four hundred years ago, the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, began building a house of God in the middle of a sacred pool in Amritsar.
Many Sikhs tell that he asked his friend, the Muslim saint Mian Mir of Lahore, to lay the first stone.
And he gave it four doors, one on every side. You could walk in from any direction.
Then Guru Arjan gathered the hymns of the Gurus into one great book, with songs by Hindu and Muslim saints in it too.
The book opens with Guru Nanak’s symbol, Ik Onkar. Ik is written as the numeral one. Onkar is an ancient name for God.
Today, at the Golden Temple, the doors still face every way, and the great book is still carried in each morning.

17.title: a song in the forest
17.told: the history and tradition of Guru Gobind Singh at Machhiwara

shots.cap: Winter, 1704. After years of war, Guru Gobind Singh had lost his home at Anandpur. His companions were scattered, and two of his sons had died in battle.
He walked alone into the forest of Machhiwara, his feet torn and bare. Tradition says he lay on the cold ground, with a lump of earth for a pillow.
And there, tradition says, he sang a hymn Sikhs still sing today: go and tell the beloved Friend how his people are.
A bed of straw with the Friend, the hymn says, is better than a palace without him.
At dawn his Sikhs found him, and two Muslim brothers, Ghani Khan and Nabi Khan, helped carry him to safety.
Sikhs call it chardi kala: ever-rising spirits. Not pretending it’s fine. Choosing which way your spirit faces, even when things fall.

18.title: a comb with a few hairs
18.told: a traditional story of Guru Gobind Singh and Pir Budhu Shah

shots.cap: In the hills lived a Muslim Sufi saint, Pir Budhu Shah, a close friend of Guru Gobind Singh. When the Guru’s people were attacked, he came to stand with them.
Afterward, the Pir found the Guru combing his long, uncut hair with a small wooden comb, as Sikhs do each morning.
Ask for anything, the Guru said. The Pir pointed to the comb, with a few hairs still caught in it. That one, please.
The Guru gave him the comb with the hair, and with it, tradition says, a small sword and a turban. His family kept them as treasures for generations.
Initiated Sikhs carry five such things, the five Ks: kesh, uncut hair. Kanga, a comb. Kara, a steel bracelet. Kachera, cotton undershorts. Kirpan, a small sword.
None is a decoration. The kirpan stands for protecting people who can’t protect themselves. The comb, for keeping hair, and life, clean and in order.

19.title: who is greater than you?
19.told: the history and tradition of Guru Tegh Bahadur, 1675

shots.cap: 1675. A group of Hindu pandits from Kashmir arrived at Anandpur, worn out. Back home, they were being forced to give up their faith.
They begged the ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, for help. He listened, and grew quiet. Tradition says he told them it would take the sacrifice of a great soul.
His son Gobind, nine years old, asked what was wrong. Then he said: who is greater than you, father, to do this?
So the Guru went to Delhi to speak for their freedom. He would not give up his faith, or let theirs be taken. There he was put to death.
Sikhs honor him as a martyr for other people’s freedom. A gurdwara, Sis Ganj, stands in Delhi where he died.
That boy became Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru. He taught that a Sikh should be sant sipahi: saint and soldier.

20.title: a coconut and five coins
20.told: the history and tradition of Nanded, 1708

shots.cap: 1708. By the river Godavari at Nanded, far in the south, Guru Gobind Singh knew his life was ending. His Sikhs gathered, wondering who would lead them next.
He had the scripture brought out: the hymns of the Gurus, first gathered by Guru Arjan a century before.
Before it he placed five coins and a coconut, the old sign of handing on the Guruship. Then he bowed.
From now on, he told them, there would be no more human Gurus. Your Guru is the Granth, the book. The Guru Granth Sahib.
So it’s treated like a revered teacher: above everyone, under a canopy. At night it’s wrapped and carried to rest. At dawn it’s opened again.

22.title: born in talwandi
22.told: the Janamsakhi tradition of Guru Nanak’s birth

shots.cap: Spring, 1469, in Punjab. A mud-brick village called Talwandi sat among the wheat fields, southwest of Lahore.
Its landlord was a Muslim, Rai Bular. His village accountant was a Hindu, Mehta Kalu. And Kalu’s wife, Mata Tripta, was about to have a baby.
The old stories say that when the baby came, the little room filled with light. The midwife, a Muslim woman named Daultan, said she’d never seen a child like him.
His big sister, Nanaki, was about five. The baby was named Nanak.
Talwandi is now called Nankana Sahib, Nanak’s town, in Pakistan. A gurdwara stands where tradition says he was born, and Sikh pilgrims still travel there.
Sikhs celebrate his birth at the autumn full moon, with lights and all-night singing, though the oldest accounts say spring. Scholars still debate it.

23.title: the sister who saw first
23.told: the Janamsakhi tradition of Bebe Nanaki

shots.cap: In Talwandi, young Nanak worried the grown-ups. He gave things away, sat silent for hours, and asked questions nobody could answer.
His father loved him and worried constantly. But his big sister, Nanaki, watched him differently. She believed in him before there was much to go on.
Nanaki married and moved to the town of Sultanpur. When her brother was a young man, drifting, she brought him there, and her husband found him work.
Some tellings say that when he set out, Nanaki gave the money for Mardana’s rabab, the instrument that would carry her brother’s songs.
Before he left, tradition says, he promised her: whenever you remember me, I’ll come. Years later, at the end of her life, he came.
Some Sikhs call Bebe Nanaki the first Sikh, the first follower of the Guru. She was his sister before she was anything else.

24.title: what do the letters mean?
24.told: a sakhi from the Janamsakhis, a traditional story

shots.cap: When Nanak was about seven, his father took him to the village teacher, the pandha, to learn his letters and one day keep accounts like his dad.
The teacher wrote the alphabet on a wooden board, a patti, and told the boy to copy it. Nanak did.
Then he asked: but what do they mean? Not what sound they make. What do they point to? The teacher had no answer.
So the boy began to explain. Each letter could point toward God. The first, toward the One who made everything. The next, toward truth. And on and on.
In the story, the teacher bowed to his student.
The scripture really holds a poem by Guru Nanak called Patti, the writing board. Each letter opens a line about God. Some think he wrote it grown up.

25.title: the cobra’s shade
25.told: a sakhi from the Janamsakhis, a traditional story

shots.cap: A hot afternoon beyond Talwandi. Young Nanak had been sent to watch the family’s buffaloes. His father hoped it would teach him responsibility.
But the boy lay down under a tree and fell asleep in the heat. Slowly the sun moved, and the shade slid off his face.
A cobra slid up beside him, raised itself, and spread its hood wide over his face, like a small umbrella.
Rai Bular, the village landlord, came riding by and saw it. He didn’t reach for a stick. He understood that this boy was under God’s protection.
From that day, Rai Bular honored the boy, and defended him to his worried father more than once.

26.title: the true bargain
26.told: a sakhi, a traditional story of Guru Nanak

shots.cap: When Guru Nanak was young, his father gave him twenty rupees and sent him to market. Make a good deal, he said. A true bargain.
On the road, Nanak met a group of holy men who had gone without food for days.
He spent every rupee on flour, lentils and ghee, and fed them all.
He came home with empty hands. His father was furious. Where’s the deal?
Nanak said feeding the hungry is the truest deal there is. Sikhs remember the place as Sacha Sauda.
Sikh tradition says that when the emperor Akbar came to see the third Guru, he first sat on the floor and ate in the row with everyone.
Today gurdwaras everywhere keep a langar, a free kitchen. Simple vegetarian food, everyone in one row on the floor, the pangat. Any faith, or none.

27.title: yours, yours, yours
27.told: a sakhi of Guru Nanak, a traditional story

shots.cap: As a young man in Sultanpur, Guru Nanak worked as a storekeeper, weighing out grain from the governor’s store.
One day he was measuring grain for a customer, counting each measure aloud: one, two, three…
At thirteen he said tera, and stopped counting. Tera, tera, he kept saying, yours, yours, and kept pouring out the grain.
Someone ran to the governor: Nanak is giving away the store! The governor ordered the accounts checked.
The clerks counted everything. Nothing was missing. In many tellings, there was even more than before.
Sikhs build a life on three pillars: naam japna, remembering God all day long. Kirat karni, honest work. And vand chakna, sharing.
One common way is simran, remembering on the breath: wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath, while you cook, drive or work.

6.title: the giant in the fog
6.told: from the life of Carl Jung

Long ago in Japan, two Zen monks, Tanzan and Ekido, were walking down a country road. The rain had turned it to mud.
At a bend they met a young woman in a silk kimono and sash. She couldn’t cross the mud without ruining it.
“Come on,” said Tanzan. He lifted her in his arms, carried her over the mud, and set her down on the other side.
Then the monks walked on. Ekido said nothing, all afternoon. But inside, he was turning it over, and over, and over.
That night, at a temple, it burst out of him. “Monks don’t go near women! Especially young, lovely ones. Why did you do that?”
Tanzan smiled. “I left her back there by the road. Are you still carrying her?”
A sharp comment at nine in the morning can still be riding with you at midnight. Thoughts arrive. You don’t have to carry them.
In Buddhist tradition, on the night of his awakening, Siddhartha sat beneath a great fig tree. He vowed not to rise until he understood.
Then came Mara, the tempter, with storms and a shadowy army, trying to drive him from his seat. Siddhartha did not move.
So Mara tried words. “This seat is mine. My army will speak for me. Who will speak for you?” Siddhartha was alone.
He didn’t argue. He let his right hand slip down over his knee, and touched the earth with his fingertips.
As the old texts tell it, the earth roared: I am his witness. And Mara’s army scattered like leaves in the wind.
By dawn the storm was gone, and Siddhartha had woken up. From then on he was called the Buddha, the one who is awake.
Today that hand reaches down in temples and homes all over the world. And your own feet are on the earth too, right now.
In France in the 1640s, a young man named Blaise Pascal built one of the first calculating machines, to help his father with tax sums.
Later, a gambler’s question about dice led him to help work out the mathematics of chance. And he watched his friends.
They gambled, they hunted, they rushed about at court. Take the hunter, said Pascal. He gallops all day after a hare.
But hand him the same hare as a gift, and he wouldn’t take it. It was never about the hare.
In an old translation of his notes: all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
Pascal died at thirty-nine. His friends gathered his scraps of notes into a book, the Pensées, which means “thoughts.”
Today the hare fits in a pocket. A waiting room, a red light, a quiet minute, and the hand goes. The chase, again.
This story is from the Talmud, the great book of Jewish teaching. A Roman emperor often talked with a Jewish sage, Rabbi Joshua.
In Jewish tradition, the Sabbath runs from Friday sundown to Saturday nightfall, a day of rest from work. The meal is cooked ahead.
One day the emperor asked him, “Why does your Sabbath food smell so wonderful?”
“We have a spice,” said the rabbi. “Its name is Shabbat. We put it in, and its fragrance fills the house.”
“Give me some!” said the emperor. He had the finest cooks in the empire.
“For one who keeps the Sabbath, it works,” said the rabbi. “For one who doesn’t keep it, it doesn’t.”
Today, for Sabbath-observant Jews, the phone is set down with the rest of the week’s work. Some others borrow the shape: one meal, phones away.

12.title: after the fire
12.told: from the First Book of Kings

shots.cap: In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Elijah was worn out and afraid. A powerful queen had threatened his life, so he ran far into the desert.
Under a lone desert tree he lay down, ready to give up. An angel woke him with bread and water, and he walked on.
He walked forty days to a holy mountain and slept in a cave. There he was told: go out, and stand on the mountain.
A great wind tore at the rocks, but God was not in the wind. Then an earthquake, then a fire. God was not in them.
And after the fire, in the old English wording, came “a still small voice.”
When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak, and went out to stand at the mouth of the cave.
Today the car, the shower and the walk to the store all get filled with sound. A quiet minute can be a mountain of its own.
In an old Daoist story, Yao, a wise emperor of legend, went looking for a hermit named Xu You, who lived simply by a river.
“When the sun and moon are out, why keep the torches burning?” said Yao. “You are the sun. Please, take my empire.”
“The tailorbird builds its nest in the deep forest,” said Xu You, “but it uses no more than one branch.”
“The mole drinks from the river, but takes no more than a bellyful. Go home, my lord. I have no use for the empire.”
In a later telling, Xu You was so unmoved by the offer that he went down to the river and washed out his ears.
Today the forest fits in a shopping cart. The glow of the new thing fades, and the wanting walks on. Xu You stopped at one branch.
In Luke’s Gospel, Jesus came to a village. Ten men with leprosy stood far off and called out: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”
He told them: go, show yourselves to the priests. A priest could declare them clean, and let them come home.
And as they went, they were healed.
One of them, seeing he was healed, turned back, praising God at the top of his voice.
He fell at Jesus’s feet and thanked him. He was a Samaritan, from a people many Jews of his day kept apart from.
“Weren’t ten made clean?” said Jesus. “Where are the nine?” Then to the man: “Get up and go. Your faith has made you whole.”
Today: the family dinner where everyone names one thing they’re thankful for. Half the table groans. It still counts. Out loud counts.

15.title: the rule that keeps turning up

shots.cap: In ancient China, about 2,500 years ago, the teacher Confucius gathered students. One of the cleverest was named Zigong.
Zigong was quick, smooth-talking and very good with money. He did well as a merchant, and was sent out as a diplomat.
One day Zigong told his teacher: “What I don’t want others to do to me, I don’t want to do to them either.”
Confucius answered: “Zigong, you have not attained to that.” Not yet.
Another day, Zigong asked: “Is there one word you could live by for your whole life?”
Confucius said: “Is not reciprocity such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.”
Today: a sharp reply typed fast, thumb over send. Would I want this sent to me? One word for a whole life, one message at a time.
In the Buddha’s time, King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika sat together one evening on the palace terrace.
The king asked her: “Mallika, is there anyone dearer to you than yourself?”
“No, great king,” she said. “No one is dearer to me than myself. And you?” He thought, and said: “No, Mallika. Not for me either.”
The king went to the Buddha and told him what they had said.
The Buddha said: search every direction with your mind, and you’ll find no one dearer to anyone than themselves.
“So,” he said, “since each person holds themselves most dear, one who loves themselves should never harm another.”
Today: the voice in the mirror after a long day. The Buddha’s reasoning starts right there. You’re dear to you. So is everyone else.
In the Mahabharata, after a great war, King Yudhishthira held a huge royal sacrifice. He gave away mountains of gold, grain and cows.
Then a mongoose appeared, half its body shining gold. It announced: this whole sacrifice is worth less than one little gift of barley flour.
Once, the mongoose said, in a famine, a poor family of four gathered just enough barley flour for one small meal, and shared it four ways.
Before they ate, a hungry guest came to the door. The old man gave him his share. Still hungry. His wife gave hers. Then their son, then his wife.
The guest was Dharma, goodness itself, in disguise, and he blessed them. The mongoose rolled in their spilled flour, and half its body turned gold.
Ever since, it has rolled at every grand sacrifice, hoping to turn the other half gold. Not even the king’s worked.
Today: a bag of rice left in a street pantry box at dusk. No one watching. That’s the kind of gift the mongoose is still looking for.
In Matthew’s Gospel, on the night before he died, Jesus ate a last supper with his friends, then walked out with them into the dark.
They came to an olive garden called Gethsemane. He took three close friends, Peter, James and John, a little further in.
“My soul is very sorrowful,” he told them. “Stay here, and keep watch with me.”
He went a little further, fell on his face, and prayed, alone.
He came back, and found them asleep.
“Could you not watch with me one hour?” he said to Peter. Then, gently: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
Today: 2 a.m., the whole building asleep. You’re not the only one awake with something heavy. Not even close.

19.title: the whole world in his mouth

shots.cap: In Hindu tradition, Krishna is God come to earth. As a toddler in a village of cowherds, he was a handful. One day the boys saw him eating dirt.
His big brother Balarama and the other boys ran to his mother, Yashoda: “Krishna ate mud!”
Yashoda took his little hand. Krishna looked up, all innocence. “I didn’t! They’re fibbing. Look in my mouth if you don’t believe me.”
She looked, and saw everything: sky and stars, mountains and oceans, fire, wind, the moon. And inside it all, her own village, and herself.
She was shaken. Was this a dream? Who was this child? Then, the old text says, he let her forget, and wrapped her in a mother’s love again.
She lifted him onto her lap and held him close. Just her little boy again, in the middle of everything.
Today: a night sky far from the city, so full of stars it looks fake. For a moment you get small, in the good way.

20.title: back before sunset
20.told: an old story of the Pythagoreans

shots.cap: In ancient Syracuse lived two friends, Damon and Phintias. They were Pythagoreans, followers of the old teacher Pythagoras. Their saying: friends have all things in common.
The ruler, Dionysius, didn’t believe friendship like that was real. His courtiers said: let’s test it.
So Phintias was accused of plotting and sentenced to die. He asked for the rest of the day to put his affairs in order.
Damon stepped forward: if Phintias didn’t return, Damon would die in his place. The court laughed. Who comes back to die?
The sun sank lower. And just before it set, Phintias came back.
Dionysius was stunned. He embraced them both, and begged to be let in as their third friend.
Today: two old friends on a park bench at sunset, a small quarrel mended before dark. The kind of friend who comes back.
In 1244, in the city of Konya, in today’s Turkey, Rumi was a respected Muslim scholar and teacher, with books, students and a fine name.
Then a wandering stranger came to town: Shams of Tabriz. In one popular telling, he found Rumi reading beside a pool.
Shams tossed the books into the water. Rumi cried out. Shams lifted them out, dry. “What is this?” Rumi asked. “Something you don’t know yet.”
The two became inseparable. Rumi’s students grew jealous. Then one day Shams was gone, and no one knows for sure what happened.
Out of the loss came an ocean of poems. His great work, the Masnavi, begins with a reed flute, crying.
The reed was cut from its reed bed. Every note it plays, Rumi says, is a song of longing to go back home.
Today his name is on poems shared on phones every day, often with his faith left out. He was a Muslim scholar, and his poems are full of the Qur’an.

22.title: the emperor under the blankets
22.told: from the notebook of Marcus Aurelius

shots.cap: Remember Marcus Aurelius, the emperor with the notebook? One cold morning, he lay under his blankets, and did not want to get up.
So he argued with himself, in writing. When you rise unwillingly, he told himself, remember: “I am rising to the work of a human being.”
“Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?” Then he answered himself: but this is more pleasant.
He looked at the little plants, the birds, the ants, the spiders, the bees, all busy doing their part to keep the world in order.
And you, a human being, he asked himself, won’t do a human’s work?
For a Stoic, a human’s work was simple to say: be kind, be fair, be useful to the people around you.
Today: the alarm, the warm covers, the bargaining. Get up, not to be impressive, but because there’s a human’s work waiting.
In the Roman Empire, almost two thousand years ago, a boy from what’s now Turkey grew up enslaved. His name, Epictetus, means “acquired.” Bought.
An old story says his master once began twisting his leg. Epictetus looked up and said, quietly: “You will break it.”
The master kept twisting, and the leg broke. Epictetus said, calmly: “Didn’t I tell you that you would break it?”
To be honest about it: this story comes from one Roman writer, Celsus. Another old source says illness made him lame. No one knows for sure.
What is known: Epictetus was lame, was freed, and became a famous teacher. He taught: “Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will.”
Today: a bad knee, a hard diagnosis, a person who won’t change. Some things aren’t yours to fix. The voice you answer in still is.

More than 2,300 years ago, a merchant named Zeno sailed from Phoenicia with a cargo of precious purple dye.
Near Athens, the ship was wrecked. The cargo, the fortune, all of it went into the sea.
Zeno made it ashore with almost nothing. He was about thirty, in a city where he knew no one.
He wandered into a bookshop and sat down. The bookseller was reading aloud from a book about Socrates.
Zeno was hooked. Socrates questioned everything, owned almost nothing, and wasn’t afraid. Zeno had lost everything, and found his life’s work.
Years later, the story goes, Zeno looked back and said: “I made a good voyage when I was shipwrecked.”
Today: the job that ended, a box of desk things, a bookshop window. Not every loss leads somewhere good. But a few pages can still change a life.

26.title: follow that man
26.told: an old story about Zeno and Crates

shots.cap: Zeno looked up from the book about Socrates and asked the bookseller: where can I find people like this, today?
Right then, a strange figure walked past the door. The bookseller pointed: “Follow that man.”
It was Crates, a Cynic philosopher. Born rich, he had given it all away, and said exactly what he thought. Zeno followed him.
But Zeno was shy. So Crates handed him a pot of lentil soup and told him to carry it through a busy part of Athens.
Zeno hid it under his cloak. Crates cracked the pot with his staff. Soup ran down Zeno’s legs, and he ran.
Crates called after him: “Why run away, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you.”
Today: coffee down your shirt on a full train. Everyone looks. Spilled soup is only spilled soup.
Zeno didn’t teach in a private school. He taught in a public place, where people passed all day: the edge of the marketplace in Athens.
He taught under a stoa, a long porch of columns. His was the painted porch, its walls covered in famous paintings of battles.
At first his followers were called Zenonians. But the name that stuck was the place: people of the stoa. The Stoics.
Anyone could stop and listen, and anyone could talk. One day a young man wouldn’t stop talking, mostly nonsense.
Zeno said: “The reason we have two ears and only one mouth is that we may listen more and talk less.”
Athens honored him for a life that matched his words. They even trusted him with the keys to the city walls.
Today: lunch in a busy plaza, a friend mid-story. Two ears, one mouth. Let them finish. Wisdom in the open.
Cleanthes was a boxer who came to Athens, the story goes, with almost no money. He wanted to study with Zeno at the painted porch.
So every night he drew water from the wells in the city’s gardens, bucket after bucket. By day, he studied.
Summoned to explain how he lived, he brought witnesses: the gardener whose water he drew, and a woman whose grain he ground.
The court was so impressed it voted him a gift of money. Zeno told him not to accept it.
Other students called him the donkey. Fine, he said: then I’m the one strong enough to carry Zeno’s load. He wrote his notes on oyster shells.
When Zeno died, the one who took over the school wasn’t the quickest student. It was Cleanthes, the water carrier.
Today: the dishes at ten at night. One plate, then the next. Not beneath you. Carry the water.
